analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 5% annual tax on billionaires' wealth to fund health care, child care, housing, and teacher raises.
analysis.headline: Introduced on March 2, 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, where it has sat without a markup or vote ever since; it has one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new annual federal tax of 5% on the total net value of assets held by anyone worth more than $1 billion, including hard-to-value private business stakes, with a 60% rate for billionaires who renounce their citizenship to escape it. It would spend the money on a broad list of programs aimed at working families: $3,000-per-person rebate checks, expanded health insurance subsidies, Medicare dental, hearing, and vision coverage, $85.6 billion a year for a housing trust fund, a universal child care entitlement for young children, a $60,000 salary floor for public school teachers, and expanded funding for home-based long-term care. The bill has gone no further than committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare (dental, hearing, and vision care starting in 2027–2028), families with children under 6 earning up to 250% of their state's median income (a child care entitlement), everyone (a $3,000 rebate, $6,000 for couples, plus $3,000 per dependent), people buying insurance on the ACA marketplaces (the income cap on premium subsidies is removed), public school teachers (a $60,000 minimum salary), renters and people needing housing assistance ($85.6 billion a year to the Housing Trust Fund), and disabled and elderly people who need home-based care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, young families, teachers, and renters

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an annual tax equal to 5% of the net value of all assets held by any individual or trust worth more than $1 billion, with married couples treated as one taxpayer and the threshold indexed to inflation.

Requires the Treasury to audit at least half of wealth-tax taxpayers each year and funds enforcement with 1% of the tax's revenue; sets a 60% tax rate for covered billionaires who expatriate, and directs the Treasury to build a registry of ownership for the assets being taxed.
Provides a $3,000 per-person affordability rebate ($6,000 for couples, plus $3,000 per dependent) for 2026.
Removes the 400%-of-poverty income cap on premium tax credits, so people at any income level can get ACA marketplace subsidies, with higher earners paying a flat 8.5% of income toward premiums.

Adds Medicare coverage of dental and oral health services (starting January 1, 2027 for dentures and 2028 for other services), hearing aids for moderately severe or worse hearing loss, audiology services, and routine eye exams and one pair of eyeglasses, with a 10% payment bonus for providers in shortage areas and a phase-in shielding Part B premiums from the dental cost from 2027 through 2031.
Authorizes $85.647 billion per year for the Housing Trust Fund for fiscal years 2026 through 2035.

Creates a birth-through-five child care entitlement for children in families up to 250% of state median income, appropriates $20 billion for local grants and Head Start awards, and requires state payment rates set from cost studies that cover providers' fixed costs and wages.
Establishes a $60,000-a-year minimum salary for every public school teacher in the United States, with collective bargaining rules.

Funds home- and community-based services improvement grants and programs, and permanently extends Medicaid protections against spousal impoverishment for home-care recipients and the Money Follows the Person demonstration.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and trusts whose net assets exceed $1 billion, who would pay 5% of that value every year on top of existing taxes, with no deduction from income tax; a billionaire who renounces US citizenship would owe 60% of their asset value in the year of departure. The tax reaches spouses jointly and counts young children's property toward the parent's total.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies each year to the total value of assets whether or not anything is sold, so an owner of a large private company could owe tax on paper value they have not cashed in; for hard-to-value assets the Treasury may allow a value based on assumed appreciation rates for similar assets, which invites disputes over valuation.

The bill's spending is very large and open-ended — $85.6 billion a year for housing, a $20 billion down payment on child care plus 'such sums as may be necessary' each year, a national teacher pay floor — and the sources contain no estimate of the wealth tax's actual revenue or of whether it would cover the cost.

Medicare dental payments would be set at 70% of the national median private dental fee, which is below what many dentists charge privately; if participation falls short, the new coverage could be hard for beneficiaries to actually use.

The bill requires a federal registry of ownership of taxable assets, including closely held business shares, and requires owners of 5% or more of a private business owned by a billionaire to report its value — a compliance burden and a level of financial disclosure the affected households have opposed in comparable proposals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad, concrete, and aimed squarely at working and middle-income households: a new cash rebate, child care, dental and hearing coverage, housing money, and a teacher pay floor. The cost falls on a tiny group of extremely wealthy households. The honest concerns are practical, not distributional: no public revenue estimate is in the record, valuing private companies every year is administratively hard, opponents have long argued an annual tax on unrealized wealth raises constitutional questions because direct taxes must be apportioned among the states, and the dental fee schedule could limit real-world access. On paper the trade favors ordinary families; whether the financing holds up is untested.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and it has sat there since with no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 2, 2026; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat, in addition to Sanders.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained from the bill itself. Because it has not moved, billionaire households would continue to pay no annual wealth tax, and the families, seniors, teachers, and renters the bill targets have received none of its benefits.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont (independent, caucuses with Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill on March 2, 2026.

for.name: A Senate Democrat (sole cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, controls whether it gets a markup or vote; the action history shows no committee action since referral.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority controlling Senate committees and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator has sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it has not been scheduled for floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is an independent who caucuses with Democrats and the only cosponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has joined, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill taxes their total net asset value at 5% every year, on top of existing taxes and with no income-tax offset, at 60% for anyone renouncing citizenship. The revenue funds the bill's benefits for ordinary families, so their interest in killing the bill runs directly against the public's interest in passing it.

industries.industry: Health insurers and ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: Removing the 400%-of-poverty cap on premium tax credits extends federal subsidies to higher earners, keeping more enrollment and subsidy dollars flowing through private marketplace plans; the bill also repeals the health subtitle of the 2025 reconciliation law (with exceptions). Expanding subsidized coverage helps people while locking private insurers in as the permanent channel for it.

Medicare dental coverage starting in 2027–2028 creates millions of new insured patients, with a 10% bonus for providers in shortage areas. But payment is set at 70% of the national median private fee, below many dentists' private rates, capping the upside.

Medicare would pay for hearing aids for moderately severe or worse hearing loss starting in 2028, a large new customer base. Payment is capped at federal supply-schedule rates and subject to competitive acquisition, limiting prices and profits.

The birth-through-five entitlement routes federal money to licensed providers, with state payment rates required to cover providers' full costs and wages under approved cost models. Providers gain a stable, government-funded customer base, and the design requires the funding to track their actual costs.

industries.industry: Home- and community-based care providers and the home care workforce
industries.note: The bill funds HCBS improvement planning grants and quality programs and permanently extends spousal-impoverishment protections and Money Follows the Person, expanding paid home-based care as an alternative to nursing homes.

Routine eye exams every two years and one pair of conventional eyeglasses would be covered starting in 2028, though payment is capped at federal supply-schedule rates and deluxe and reading glasses are excluded.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the profile of a statement bill: one sponsor and one cosponsor, referred to Finance on day one, and no committee action since. Unless the Finance chair schedules a markup or leadership attaches pieces of it to a larger tax or spending package — neither of which the record shows any movement toward — it is very likely to sit in committee and expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, without ever getting a vote.
